Hello Council Member Valdemoros, I'm writing today in solidarity with other concerned residents of your district to ask you to consider the mayor's budget for FY '21/'22. As I'm sure you're aware, the current recommended budget allocates upwards of $80 million to the Salt Lake City Police Department. I would like to encourage you to defund the police department by 50% in order to reprioritize our city's financial priorities in favor of supportive housing, mental health resources and harm reduction programming. I ask that you strongly consider the following specific changes: * Reduce the number of police and administrative personnel in the SLCPD by 50%, from 711 full-time employees (FTEs) to 356. * Reduce the police department budget by 50%, from $79 million to $39.5 million. * Take steps to eliminate the funding from the non-departmental budget and other departments reserved for policing operations. * Invest the funds diverted from the police department into supportive community programs. I am sure that you are aware of the current headlines and statistics about increases in crime nation-wide over the course of the last year, and I have no doubt that you're concerned about violent crime especially. I am also concerned. While others in the city may believe these concerns will be addressed by increasing police funding by 5.4 % from last year - I have to ask that you resist this fear mongering that prioritizes criminalization and incarceration over equity and public safety. The safest communities are not the most policed, the most surveilled, or the most ticketed. The safest communities are the communities with the most resources, including not just money, but also the social infrastructure to thrive and demonstrate resilience in hard times. Our communities do not have affordable housing - we have wealthy developers with access to people in power. Our communities do not have living wages, or comprehensive affordable healthcare - we have low paying jobs that disproportionately exploit people with historically marginalized identities. Our communities do not accessible trash cans, public restrooms, showers, harm reduction services or accessible free transportation - we have bulldozers, jails and a state culture of displacement and violence. Divest in the police, invest in our community. All the best, Mike Braak District 4 Resident

Hello, My name is Gary Bowen and I work for Cotopaxi located on 74 South Main. The homeless situation continues to worsen and we need an action plan on resolving the problem. Our employees are getting more nervous about heading into the office as well as potential customers of our retail store at the street level (corporate offices are upstairs). There have been numerous instances that I've witnessed and have been reported by our employees including homeless people doing drugs, having their pants pulled down exposing themselves, the filth on the sidewalk, shouting profanities at each other at times (homeless to homeless), trash left by homeless people, aggressive panhandling. These behaviors make it difficult for our retail store to conduct business, for our customers to come in, retail store employees to feel safe and for our employees to come down to the office. I realize this is a challenging problem. Many of the people on Main are mentally ill. The Starbucks attracts a lot of the homeless (nothing against Starbucks). Are there laws against loitering? What options are being considered? I'm very interested to hear what the latest plans are to deal with it. Respectfully, the current situation can't continue or we will lose the downtown area. Thanks for your time. Respectfully, Gary Bowen

In the council's consideration of a new budget, I urge you to consider the damage inflicted on the police department by the city council and mayor during the past 12 months. Since you cannot retain officers through your "competitive benefits" package, I urge you to consider cash bonuses paid over a 3 year period. Consider a lump sum of $20,000 per officer: $5,000 upon hire, $5,000 upon completion of the academy, $5,000 upon completion of probation and $5,000 at the end of three years. Given how morale has plummeted, this is likely the only way to retain officers for a decent period of time. Thank you, William Woods

The three things we've had problems with in my neighborhood (Fairpark) are a large number of people living on the street or in other public spaces, litter, and theft. We've had our car broken into twice and a package stolen within the last year. There is a lot of litter on the street and in the park, including occasionally used needles. I'm worried for my son's safety, and my dog is always trying to eat (and does eat when I am not quick enough to stop him) discarded food, including chocolate. Worse of all are the people who are living in terrible conditions. A woman two blocks up died of carbon monoxide poisoning trying to keep warm in her tent. I was stopped by a woman who said she was freezing (literally) and had nowhere to go. She wasn't making a whole lot of sense. Unfortunately, I had no idea how to help her. Another man stopped me one time without shoes on in the dead of winter. I tried to give him an old but functional pair of my husband's, but he just swore at me. Please, put all the resources you can into addiction help, mental health care, and housing, and also into law enforcement. We need to provide the help these people need, and people like me also have a right to a safe environment. People don't belong on the streets. Camilla

Due to our position as Utah's capital city, we disportionally experience protest movements and rallies. We also have a homeless problem with a lot of population growth. Being a police officer is a hard, dangerous job. Each member of our police force deserves to be appropriately compensated and supported in their work. Additionally, I support the elevation of the SLC Parks and Public lands to a department level position. I want to see our Parks and Public Lands play a larger role in city government. A department level position will permit the Director to set policy and objectives around the department instead of within the Department of Utilities. Hi, I noticed on the meeting agenda for today that there is an item concerning the Station Center area of the city. The idea of that district becoming the premiere transit-oriented district in the state is an exciting one, and I love the idea of having a university presence there. I appreciate the RDA's efforts in getting all of this off the ground but I have to make a comment concerning the Rio Grande Depot. In past presentations up until and including today's, the old station has been considered a "barrier to development." I know that members of the city council and RDA have seen the plan to make the Rio Grande Depot the centerpiece rail station of the entire Utah rail transit network by digging a cut-and-cover trench for trains under the 500 W right-of-way and opening the old railyards to development. Said plan is reminiscent of Denver's Union Station redevelopment and I think would have comparable positive economic and urban impacts for Salt Lake City. I would love to hear what members of the RDA have to say about this idea, its feasibility, and whether or not there have been discussions to incorporate into existing plans for Station Center. Thanks! Matthew Givens
